title: 2  Purpose of Report
text:
2.1 Questions and Requests for Information
Orange County respectfully acknowledges that every data point in this report represents a human life and the loss of a loved one. The purpose of this report is to help our communities, and their leaders, develop a deeper understanding of the circumstances surrounding drug overdose deaths to inform community level overdose prevention efforts.
This report is a joint effort between the Office of the Medical Examiner, the Department of Mental Health, and the Department of Health in Orange County, NY. It provides data on overdose deaths and examines trends by drug type to provide local context to the current drug overdose landscape. It includes all overdose deaths in Orange County between January 1 and December 31, 2025.
The report aims to: - Provide annual data on fatal overdoses to local planning partners - Analyze trends in drug type, demographics, and location - Inform community level overdose prevention and response programs
For any questions regarding this report or use of the data contained within, please contact the Orange County Department of Health, Division of Epidemiology and Public Health Planning: - Phone: 845-291-2330 - Email: epidemiology@orangecountygov.com

title: 3  Methods
text:
Skip to main content




Drug Classification: For the purpose of this report, target drug compounds found in post-mortem toxicology reports were classified into select groups before being represented in graph form. In some instances, metabolites produced by the body during drug metabolism are classified under their corresponding parent drug category. For example, the metabolite cocaethylene, which forms only in the body if both alcohol and cocaine are consumed at the same time, is classified as both alcohol and cocaine. The visuals in this report are always titled to make clear whether they display a count of a specific drug or a count of the drug classification. See Appendix A for drug classification breakdowns.
Overdose Deaths: The Orange County Office of the Medical Examiner (OCOME) investigates sudden, unexpected, and unnatural fatalities in Orange County to ensure accurate cause and manner of death certification. Death investigations conducted by the OCOME include, but are not limited to, any death that is not due to 100% natural causes, deaths occurring as a result of workplace injury, deaths that are unattended by a physician, deaths resulting from homicides or suicides, and any deaths in which injury is a contributing factor (this includes acute drug intoxication and overdoses). For suspected overdose deaths, OCOME staff collect specimens for toxicological analysis to determine which substances may have contributed to the death. Other complex tests may also be required. Because these procedures can take 8 to 12 weeks or longer to complete, the final report cannot be finalized until all data are gathered and testing reports are finished.
OCOME is required to investigate deaths that occur in Orange County so this report may include non-residents. The report does not include residents that died of an overdose outside of Orange County. Suspected Overdoses: The Overdose Detection Mapping Application Program (ODMAP) provides current suspected overdose data across Orange County. Overdose data are recorded on scene by first responders including: local police departments, county police, state police, or emergency medical services and entered into ODMAP by staff at the Hudson Valley Crime Analysis Center. These are considered “suspected” overdoses because they have not been confirmed by a medical professional. However, monitoring these local trends in emergency response to suspected overdose can ensure local resources can be mobilized effectively.

When applicable, rates are used instead of raw counts to allow for meaningful comparisons across different population sizes, such as between age groups
Population rates utilize the 2023 5-Year American Community Survey (ACS) from the US Census Bureau
Using the ACS 5-Year dataset provides annual updates while ensuring a smaller margin of error
This approach maximizes accuracy and reliability, particularly when analyzing smaller geographic areas

title: 5  Definitions
text:
Skip to main content




Drug Overdose: The Office of the Medical Examiner conducts autopsies and examinations to determine if toxic concentrations or combinations of drugs were present in the body and contributed to the fatality. If drugs are deemed contributory, they are listed in the cause of death statement and included in the annual overdose data. Deaths included in this report reflect both accidental and suicidal (intentional) overdoses. They are also referred to as “overdose deaths” or “overdose mortality.”
Benzodiazepines: Colloquially known as benzos, benzodiazepines are a class of depressant drugs prescribed to treat conditions such as anxiety disorders, insomnia, or seizures. Common benzodiazepines include Xanax, Valium, Ativan, and Klonopin. For this report, benzodiazepines have been separated from their larger classification of central nervous system depressant due to the high prevalence of their misuse and their high potential for dependency.
Cannabis: Cannabis or cannabinoids refers to the dried leaves, flowers, stems, and seeds of the cannabis plant, which can be smoked, vaped, or consumed as an edible food or beverage. While there are many chemical compounds within the plant, tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) is the primary psychoactive compound that produces a high. Other names include marijuana, pot, grass, weed, and hash.
Central Nervous System Depressants: Central nervous system (CNS) depressants are medications used to treat anxiety, panic attacks, seizures, and insomnia. They slow down brain activity causing muscles to relax and leading to feelings of drowsiness, relaxation, and reduced inhibitions. Common CNS depressants include benzodiazepines (Valium, Klonopin, Xanax), barbiturates (phenobarbital, Nembutal), and sleep aids (Ambien, Lunesta, and Sonata).
Cocaethylene: Cocaethylene is a toxic, psychoactive substance created automatically by the liver when cocaine and alcohol (ethanol) are consumed together.
Dissociative Anesthetics/Hallucinogens: These are psychoactive drugs that alter a person’s perception, mood, or cognition, often causing people to feel separated from their body or experience an altered state of consciousness. Common dissociative anesthetics are Ketamine, PCP (phencyclidine), nitrous oxide, and dextromethorphan, and in addition to an altered sense of perception they can also have a sedation effect in users. Common hallucinogens include LSD (lysergic acid diethylamide), mescaline, psilocybin, PCP, ecstasy, and ketamine.
Ethanol: Ethanol refers to a colorless volatile flammable liquid that is the main intoxicating agent in liquors and is also used as a solvent and in fuel.
Medetomidine: Medetomidine is a potent, short-acting alpha-2 agonist used as a non-opioid sedative for analgesic and muscle-relaxant effects. Its pharmacological effects are similar to those of xylazine. Like xylazine, medetomidine is increasingly found as an adulterant in illicit substances.
Medications for Opioid Use Disorder [MOUD]: Sometimes referred to as Medication-Assisted Treatment, US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved Medications for Opioid Use Disorder include buprenorphine, methadone, and naltrexone. Brand names for these medications include Suboxone, Sublocade, Zubsolv, Methadose, and Vivitrol. These drugs interact with opioid receptors in the brain to ease withdrawal symptoms and cravings while preventing any other opioid from taking effect. MOUD remains the most effective, evidence-based treatment for Opioid Use Disorder.
Mitragynine (Kratom): Mitragynine is the primary psychoactive alkaloid found in the Southeast Asian plant Mitragyna speciosa, commonly known as kratom. It acts as a partial opioid receptor agonist and is consumed for its stimulant-like effects in small doses and its pain-relieving, sedative effects in larger doses.
Naloxone: Often known by its brand name, Narcan, naloxone is an FDA-approved medication designed to rapidly reverse the effects of an opioid overdose. As an opioid antagonist, naloxone will not reverse the effects of non-opioid substances.
Opioids: Opioids are a class of natural, semi-synthetic, or synthetic drugs used to reduce pain by attaching to opioid receptors in the brain and other organs to decrease the intensity of pain signals. Common opioids include morphine, heroin, codeine, oxycodone, and fentanyl. For this report, opioids have been separated from the broader CNS Depressant category due to the prevalence of their misuse and their high potential for dependency.
Other Drugs: The expansive scope of postmortem toxicology testing captures a wide array of drugs and medications present at the time of death, including compounds that may be deemed non-contributory to the fatality. For this report, only those drugs directly contributory to the overdose death are listed. Medicinal drugs found to be non-contributory—such as blood pressure medications, supplements, or anticoagulants—are excluded.
Prescription Opioids: These medications are primarily used to manage and treat moderate to severe pain. While generally safe when taken for a short time as prescribed by a doctor, they can be misused. Prescription opioids are tracked in this data regardless of whether they were explicitly prescribed to the decedent. Common examples include hydrocodone, oxycodone, oxymorphone, morphine, and codeine.
Rate: A rate measures the frequency with which an event occurs in a defined population over a specified period. Rates are used to normalize raw counts against the overall size of the population.
Stimulants: This term covers a broad class of drugs that increase central nervous system activity. It includes prescription medications like Ritalin and Adderall, as well as illicit substances such as methamphetamine, cocaine, and crack cocaine. Stimulants carry a high potential for dependency and overdose; when mixed with opioids, they significantly increase the risk of overdose mortality.
Xylazine: Xylazine is a tranquilizer, pain reliever, and central nervous system depressant that is approved by the FDA for veterinary medicine but not approved for human use. It is increasingly found as an adulterant in the illicit drug supply. For this report, xylazine has been separated from the CNS Depressant category due to its rising presence in the illicit drug supply and the distinct challenges it presents in reversing and preventing overdoses.

title: 6  Data
text:
Skip to main content




Source: Washington/Baltimore HIDTA (n.d.) Overdose Detection Mapping Application Program (ODMAP)
The Overdose Detection Mapping Application Program (ODMAP) provides near-real-time, suspected overdose data across jurisdictions to support public safety and public health efforts to mobilize an immediate response to a sudden increase, or spike, in overdose events. ODMAP links first responders and relevant record management systems to a mapping tool to track overdoses geographically. Because first responders gather this information on-scene, these incidents are considered “suspected” overdoses until a medical diagnosis can be made. These suspected overdoses include both fatal and non-fatal events.
In Figure 1, each circle on the map represents a single suspected non-fatal overdose, and each diamond represents a single suspected fatal overdose. The color of each marker indicates the administration and amount of Naloxone used, as detailed in the accompanying legend.
The suspected overdoses in Orange County often occur in clusters, with a majority (69.3%) occurring in just three ZIP codes: 12550, 10940, and 10950. While this trend of concentrated clusters has persisted, there has been a shift in the most affected areas. This shift is driven mainly by a sharp rise in overdoses within the 10950 ZIP code (+57.1%) and a large decline in the 12771 ZIP code (-52.4%). Additionally, the trends within each of those clusters vary. The 12550 ZIP code remained at the top of the list in both 2024 and 2025, experiencing a 28.9% increase in overdoses during that time. Conversely, the second most affected ZIP code, 10940, saw a 20.2% decrease while still remaining second highest on the list. From these clusters, the data shows overdoses spreading outward, primarily following the major highway corridors that run through the county; Interstates 84 and 87, and New York State Route 17.





Figure 6.1: Suspected Overdoses by Zip Code, 2024 vs. 2025


                            
                                            




Figure 6.1 shows the suspected overdoses by ZIP Code. From 2024 to 2025, six of the county’s ten most affected ZIP codes saw an increase in suspected overdoses: 12550 (28.9% increase), 10950 (54.5% increase), 10941; (7.4% increase), 12553 (19% increase), 12549 (37.5% increase); and 12589 (150% increase). At the same time, two of the county’s cities and largest population centers saw declines. The 10940 ZIP code, which includes the City of Middletown, experienced a 20.1% decrease, while the 12771 ZIP code, including the City of Port Jervis, saw the county’s largest decrease at 52.4%.
ODMAP does have some limitations regarding the data it provides. Because suspected overdoses are recorded mainly by first responders on scene, an incident may not be captured if 911 is not called following an overdose. Additionally, an event will not be recorded if the responding agency fails to input the incident into ODMAP or does not share the resulting data with the Hudson Valley Crime Analysis Center. Despite these limitations, ODMAP remains our best tool for understanding—in near-real-time—where we are experiencing increased overdose-related activity.





Figure 6.2: Overdose Deaths by Year, 2021–2024


                            
                                            




Figure 6.2 shows that Orange County has had a continuous, year-over-year reduction in annual overdose fatalities since 2022. Total annual deaths decreased by 53.1% over this four-year period, dropping from a peak of 143 deaths in 2022 to a period low of 67 deaths in 2025. This represents 76 fewer deaths in 2025 compared to the peak in 2022.





Figure 6.3: Overdose Deaths by Quarter and Year, 2021–2024


                            
                                            




Figure 6.3 shows the annual overdose fatalities by quarter, illustrating how seasonal patterns have shifted along with an overall decline in deaths. In 2022, overdose deaths remained consistently elevated across the first three quarters before experiencing a decline in the fourth quarter. The highest single-quarter death total for the entire four-year period occurred in the second quarter of 2023, peaking at 46 deaths, which was followed by a period-wide low of 15 deaths in the third quarter. By 2024 and 2025, quarterly fluctuations were more stable, with no single quarter exceeding 22 fatalities. Most notable was the first quarter of 2025 with only 9 recorded overdose deaths, marking the first time in four years that fatalities dropped to single digits.





Figure 6.4: Rate of Overdose Deaths per 100,000 Population by Year 2021–2024


                            
                                            




Figure 6.4 displays the overdose deaths with the population-adjusted mortality rates, showing a continuous decline in the rate of overdose deaths per 100,000 residents from 2022 through 2025. The overdose rate peaked at 35.6 per 100,000 in 2022 and then dropped to 28.7 per 100,000 in 2023. This downward trend continued to sharply decline in 2024 dropping to 19.3 per 100,000 and then reaching the period low 16.6 deaths per 100,000 in 2025. Over this four-year period, the population overdose mortality rate in Orange County decreased by 53.4%.





Figure 6.5: Rate of Overdose Deaths by Sex and Year per 100,000 Population, 2021–2024


                            
                                            




Figure 6.5 displays the overdose deaths with the population-adjusted mortality rates broken down by sex from 2022 to 2025. Both groups experienced continuous, year-over-year declines throughout the four-year period, though a significant sex disparity persisted. The overdose death rate for males dropped from a peak of 51.8 per 100,000 in 2022 and then fell to 39.7 in 2023. This downward trend continued to sharply decline in 2024, dropping to 26.3 per 100,000 and then reaching the period low of 23.8 in 2025. This was a total decrease of 54.1% over four years. Similarly, the rate for females decreased from 19.0 per 100,000 in 2022 to 17.8 in 2023. A sharp decline was noted in 2024 with a rate of 10.9 per 100,000 followed by the period low of 7.9 in 2025, representing a 58.4% decline over four years. Despite these substantial reductions, the male overdose mortality rate remained about three times higher than the female rate in 2025.





Figure 6.6: Rate of Overdose Deaths by Age Group and Year per 100,000 Population, 2021–2024


                            
                                            




Figure 6.6 displays the overdose deaths with the population-adjusted mortality rates broken down by age from 2022 to 2025. Over this four-year period, every age group experienced an overall decline in mortality rates, though substantial disparities remained between generations. The 35 to 44 age group consistently experienced the highest mortality burden, dropping from a peak of 71.8 per 100,000 in 2022 to 68.4 in 2023, 40.2 in 2024, and a period low of 36.2 in 2025. The 45 to 54 age group followed a similar trend, falling from 59.2 per 100,000 in 2022 to a period low of 25.2 in 2025. For the Over 55 demographic, a dramatic drop occurred early in the time period, falling sharply from 51.0 per 100,000 in 2022 to 28.3 in 2023, before stabilizing between 21.0 and 22.8 in the final two years. The slight increase noted in this older group in 2025 was driven primarily by the 55-64 age group. Conversely, residents Under 35 consistently maintained the lowest rates in the county, fluctuating around 10.9 per 100,000 in 2022 and 2023 before dropping to a period low of 5.2 in 2025. Notably, 2025 marked the first time in four years that no deaths were reported in the 0-25 age group.





Figure 6.7: Type of Drugs Present at Time of Overdose Death, 2022–2024


                            
                                            




Figure 6.7 displays the distribution of overdose deaths by substance classification in 2025, illustrating the relative contribution of opioids, stimulants, and other substances. The most frequently identified drug classification in 2025 was cocaine, with 41 fatalities (61.2%) having cocaine or its metabolites present. Fentanyl and its analogues were the next highest classification, detected in 36 deaths (53.7%). This represents a notable shift from previous local trends where fentanyl consistently ranked as the leading drug classification in overdose mortality. Despite this shift, opioids as a broader category remain the most prevalent drug type, followed closely by all stimulants. While not a majority, alcohol and benzodiazepines were also present in a large share of overdose fatalities (29.9% and 20.9%, respectively).





Figure 6.8


                            
                                            




Figure 6.8 outlines the ten drugs most commonly present in the body at time of death for 2025, compared to their frequency in 2024. A marked shift in substance prevalence occurred between the two years. Most notably, the data reveals a 5.3% decline in deaths where fentanyl was identified and a 7.1% increase in cases involving cocaine. This trend has been developing since 2023, a year in which Orange County saw 115 overdose deaths; that year, fentanyl appeared in 75.9% of toxicology reports while cocaine appeared in 42.2%. This ongoing shift pushed cocaine past fentanyl as the single substance most frequently found in the body at the time of death in 2025. Ethanol (20.9% of deaths) and cocaethylene (11.9% of deaths) emerged as the third and fourth most frequently identified substances in 2025. Ethanol is an active ingredient in alcoholic beverages, and cocaethylene is a highly toxic metabolite formed in the body when cocaine and alcohol are consumed at the same time. Due to the incredibly short metabolic half-life of cocaine, cocaethylene is often identified in toxicologic panels even after cocaine itself has cleared the system. In addition to its longer half-life, cocaethylene is itself a toxic substance, presenting a 25-fold increase in the risk of fatal heart failure. The prominent ranking of these two substances further emphasizes the increase in localized cocaine use and underscores the heightened risk of fatal overdose when combining alcohol with other substances. Another emerging trend is the rise in mitragynine, commonly known as kratom. While kratom itself is not structurally classified as an opioid, when taken in larger quantities, it can act in a similar way to other opioids, leading to tolerance, physical dependence, and withdrawal symptoms. In December 2025, New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed a public health law prohibiting the sale of kratom products to individuals under 21 years of age, and requiring manufacturers of these products to include a prominent consumer warning label on their packaging. Orange County partners, including the Tri-County Prevention Partnership, were instrumental in advocating for and assisting in the passing of this legislation. Along with these state-level efforts, providers in Orange County are combating this growing concern by working to educate the public on the effects and potential dangers of emerging substances including kratom and kratom-derived products. These efforts are further detailed later in this report. At the same time, a decrease has been noted across both Orange County and New York State in the prevalence of xylazine found in both toxicology reports and street-level drug checking programs. However, in December of 2025, the New York State Department of Health issued an urgent public health alert1 warning of a significant statewide surge in medetomidine, a similar but higher-strength veterinary sedative, within the illicit drug supply. New York State’s drug checking programs noted an increase in medetomidine being found, rising from 4% of samples tested in 2024 to 38% of samples tested in 2025. This is an emerging trend, and medetomidine is not currently included in standard toxicology reports. Without a localized drug checking program in Orange County to track this, it is presumed that the observed decrease in xylazine is likely accompanied by the increase in medetomidine that is being seen statewide.





Figure 6.9: Percent of Overdose Deaths by Opioid and Stimulant Involvement, 2021–2024

title: 7  Current Substance Use Disorder and Overdose Prevention Efforts in Orange County
text:
7.1 WELCOME Orange
WELCOME Orange is a community-driven collaboration dedicated to promoting healthy living in Orange County through the leadership and cooperation of multidisciplinary service providers. Its mission is to create a welcoming, person-centered environment where individuals can easily access resources that support their health and well-being. By working together, participating agencies align their goals, share best practices, and speak with a unified voice to improve outcomes for those seeking assistance. This initiative fosters a seamless experience across all partner organizations, ensuring efficient service delivery and empowering individuals to achieve their goals. Ultimately, WELCOME Orange serves as the umbrella under which Orange County and its partners unite to serve the community.

section: 7.2 Changing the Orange County Addiction Treatment Ecosystem
text:
7.2 Changing the Orange County Addiction Treatment Ecosystem
In 2017, the Orange County Department of Mental Health launched a major initiative to find gaps in the local substance use treatment system. This project, called “Changing the Orange County Addiction Treatment Ecosystem,” brought together nearly 200 stakeholders from government, healthcare, and addiction treatment. Through seven intensive workshops, stakeholders identified more than 70 challenges, including a major lack of coordinated care for adolescents and pregnant patients. The resulting report laid the groundwork for expanding local treatment options. Today, this foundation drives ongoing efforts to fight the opioid crisis through community education, evidence-based treatments, and continuous system improvements.
Since this launch, new projects have further strengthened the partnership between Orange County and its local service agencies. These initiatives continue to drive system-wide changes across the local addiction and mental health landscape. Specifically, four dedicated workgroups were formed to advance the goals of the original “Ecosystem” project—

7.2.1 Community Alliance for Prevention (CAP) Workgroup
The Community Alliance for Prevention (CAP) workgroup is compiled of multiple stakeholders from different facets of prevention but primarily from the substance use field. The CAP group meets regularly and discusses the progress being made by the local community coalitions that are spread throughout Orange County. The group is responsible for keeping prevention messaging across Orange County cohesive, evidence-based, and culturally relevant and appropriate. CAP coordinates activities with schools, local police departments, and other relevant stakeholders to promote prevention efforts aimed at reducing substance misuse in children, teens, and young adults and ultimately reduce the opioid burden in Orange County. Most recently, CAP led an effort to perform the Community Level Youth Development Evaluation (CLYDE) at several school districts within the county to better evaluate the students perception of harm and risk.


7.2.2 Data Workgroup
This specialized team brings members together quarterly to review local and regional drug trends, syndromic surveillance and overdose data. The group actively refines data collection methods to better understand and explain shifting local trends. Additionally, members develop new assessment tools and protocols to expand data sharing across Orange County. These collaborative efforts directly shaped the selection of data points featured throughout this report.


7.2.3 Overdose Education and Naloxone Distribution (OEND) Workgroup
This team unites overdose prevention providers to identify regional gaps in education and naloxone access. Members share staff and resources to host public training sessions for local businesses and community groups. Notably, the workgroup has facilitated the deployment of over 250 wall-mounted naloxone boxes across Orange County. Since assuming the responsibilities of the former Communications Workgroup, the team also creates and distributes public health messaging regarding substance use.


7.2.4 Persons With Lived Experience (PWLE) Workgroup
This group consists of individuals who self-identify as having lived experience with substance use disorders. While many members work within the field of SUD treatment or prevention, professional alignment is not a requirement. Recently, the group focused on hosting regular “Peer Roundtable” events across the county. These forums allow people who use drugs and frontline workers to collectively discuss systemic barriers to care and recovery. Ultimately, these insights help shape future interventions to close local service gaps. To date, the workgroup has hosted roundtables in Newburgh, Port Jervis, Middletown, and the Village of Walden, with plans to expand into other county corridors.

text:
7.3 Non-Fatal Overdose Outreach Team
The non-fatal overdose (NFO) team is a peer run initiative funded through OCDMH to provide ongoing support to those that have experienced a non-fatal overdose. The NFO team was created in 2021 as a key strategy to engage individuals into treatment, who might otherwise not be ready to accept help. While medical personnel and emergency responders are first on the scene following an overdose, the individuals who experienced the overdose are not always ready to accept the help in that immediate aftermath. The NFO team follows up in person 24-48 hours after learning of a non-fatal overdose with a two-person peer led team and resources in hand. This timeframe is recommended as best-practice for post-overdose follow up by New York State. Furthermore, people are more receptive to accepting help from peer advocates than first responders. The NFO team works to engage the client and get them into treatment or to provide other supports as necessary. They also provide follow-up after the client has completed inpatient treatment or while they are attending outpatient treatment.

7.4 Opioid Settlement Funds
Orange County is a recipient of Opioid Settlement Funds, which stem from legal settlements between local and state governments and companies involved in manufacturing or dispensing of prescription opioids. These funds are dedicated to supporting states, counties, and municipalities in opioid prevention, treatment, recovery, and harm reduction efforts. In 2025, Orange County invested these dollars across several key areas: $499,718 for the treatment continuum, $200,000 for housing initiatives, $203,287 for priority population interventions, and $921,630 for prevention efforts; totaling $1,824,636 invested back into the community in 2025 alone. More information on the disbursement of these funds can be found on the NYS Office of Addiction Services and Supports webpage.1



New York State Office of Addiction Services and Supports, “Opioid Settlement Fund Regional Abatements,” last modified September 25, 2025, https://oasas.ny.gov/opioid-settlement-fund-regional-abatements↩︎

text:
7.5 Education and Prevention Efforts
Orange County is dedicated to making sure that both field professionals and the general public are educated on substance use disorders, even as the trends evolve at a rapid pace. Collaborative partnerships with numerous local agencies have enabled the county to host vital webinars on emerging public health topics. This includes a four-part virtual learning series focused on xylazine and wound-care practices for frontline workers serving affected populations. In conjunction with these educational sessions, the Orange County Department of Mental Health (OCDMH) purchased medical supplies to assemble specialized wound-care kits for individuals suffering from xylazine-associated skin lesions. Furthermore, the department actively distributes Naloxone kits along with advanced testing strips to detect xylazine, medetomidine, nitazenes, and fentanyl.
OCDMH also hosts a bimonthly meeting for prescribers and dispensers of Medication for Opioid Use Disorders (MOUD). This forum allows providers to discuss systemic barriers and shared successes in managing MOUD patient care. Whenever possible, OCDMH invites external organizations to present on critical and timely topics. Recent presenters include the Upstate Poison Control Center, the Opioid Response Network, and the Opioid Response Strategy. These external experts share their expertise on emerging substances and evidence-based clinical practices for treating individuals impacted by these trends and substance use.
Beyond professional development, significant efforts are directed toward educating the general public. OCDMH hosts regular Naloxone training sessions, both by request and as a standing monthly training, where participants learn to recognize and respond to opioid overdoses while reviewing current regional drug trends and local data. The Mid-Hudson Prevention Resource Center (MHPRC) and local community coalitions actively work to keep both youth and the broader public informed about emerging substances. Through specialized community scan trainings, youth coalition members and local schools learn to identify how products like kratom are marketed and advertised in gas stations and local businesses, building critical awareness of these access points. Moving forward, these initiatives will continue to expand, ensuring that local coalitions and grassroots prevention providers utilize up-to-date data and evidence-based practices.

text:
7.6 Annual Substance Use Disorder Summits
Since 2023, the Orange County Department of Mental Health, in partnership with the Orange County District Attorney’s office, SUNY Orange, the Alcohol and Drug Awareness Council of Orange County, and Orange County Stop DWI, has hosted a local summit dedicated to pressing issues in the field of substance use disorders. The first summit, held in September of 2023, focused on fentanyl and its analogues, emphasizing the role these potent synthetic substances played in the sharp incline of nationwide overdose deaths between 2019 and 2023. The following year, the focus shifted to legal substances and the consequences of their use. This timely topic aligned with the opening of cannabis dispensaries across New York State and Orange County, as well as the concurrent uptick in Driving While Intoxicated arrests. This forum also provided an avenue to discuss alcohol and other substance often perceived as less dangerous; including kratom, nitrous oxide, and synthetic cannabis products.
The most recent summit highlighted the core philosophies of WELCOME Orange, focusing on co-occurring substance use and mental health disorders. As the largest event to date, it drew 144 individuals representing 68 different agencies. The summit featured two keynote speakers and three separate breakout sessions. These sessions focused on the prevention of co-occurring disorders, the intersection of criminal justice and mental health/substance use treatment systems, and a diverse case study used to identify systemic gaps and available resources for individuals with co-occurring disorders.

section: 7.7 Expanding the Scope of Opioid-Related Data Collection
text:
7.7 Expanding the Scope of Opioid-Related Data Collection
In recent years, significant progress has been made to expand the scope and capabilities of local substance use data collection. This report was developed through a strategic partnership among Orange County’s Department of Health (OCDOH), the Office of the Medical Examiner, and the Department of Mental Health (OCDMH). This interagency collaboration has greatly enhanced the county’s ability to track emerging drug trends, deploy targeted harm reduction resources, and coordinate overdose responses.
Because OCDOH is required to complete a Community Health Assessment and Community Health Improvement Plan every five years, the county has an opportunity to gather health-related data from the community at regular intervals. While most of these surveys focus on general wellness, Orange County has made a concerted effort to collect more information related to behavioral health and substance use. Furthermore, this data collection now prioritizes the underlying social determinants of health that drive most outcomes in both behavioral and physical health. In addition, OCDMH is required to complete a behavioral health assessment of both the public and professional communities. The department is actively working to ensure relevant, impactful data are captured through surveying, as well as through the regular monitoring and oversight of partner agencies funded with county dollars.
As the partnership between OCDOH and OCDMH continues to grow, both agencies are pursuing additional sources of behavioral health data. A priority is optimizing how the county utilizes and shares data across local, state, and national networks. Specifically, partners are working to integrate insights from the Electronic Syndromic Surveillance System,2 the National Emergency Medical Services Information System,3 and the Overdose Detection Mapping Application Program4 to build a more comprehensive and unified response system.

title: 8  Appendix: Live Data Objects Example
text:
8.2 To add your own indicator

Copy an indicator sheet (Poverty Rate or Total Households).
Set the config cells in column A/B - especially Name, Table/Figure/Both (figure or table), Object ID, and (for figures) Figure Type / X Column.
Fill the data to the right of the Enter Data cell: the row-label column (col F) plus value columns, with per-column format codes in the row just above.
Add the indicator to the Master roster (optional, for tracking).
Reference it in any chapter with {{< include _generated/objects/<object_id>.qmd >}} (e.g. fig-<id> or tbl-<id>), run the generator once, then quarto render.

See scripts/WORKBOOK_SCHEMA.md and scripts/PIPELINE_USAGE.md for full details.
